cards.explanation: The answer is that He restored Jacob from captivity. Right in the first verse: "You restored Jacob from captivity." Here Jacob stands for God's people. The sons of Korah, who wrote this song, open by remembering what the LORD already did (Psalm 85:1). Good news like that is worth telling twice.

The answer is that He forgave it, friends: "You forgave the iniquity of Your people…" Iniquity is a heavy word, and the verse puts forgiveness right beside it. The singers put it right in the song. Then comes the word Selah, which I take as a spot to pause and let it sink in (Psalm 85:2).

The answer is False, friends. The text says, "You withheld all Your fury; You turned from Your burning anger." Not a little of it, not most of it. All of it (Psalm 85:3). One tiny word, and it changes the whole line.

The answer is His displeasure toward them. The sons of Korah pray, "Restore us, O God of our salvation, and put away Your displeasure toward us." They call Him the God of their salvation, and then they ask (Psalm 85:4). I think it takes real trust to ask that plainly.

The answer is True. They really ask it: "Will You be angry with us forever?" The next question is just as bold: "Will You draw out Your anger to all generations?" (Psalm 85:5). Straight to Him, no tiptoeing. The song has room for the honest question.

The word is rejoice, friends. "Will You not revive us again, that Your people may rejoice in You?" (Psalm 85:6). The revival has a purpose in the song: rejoicing in Him. I think a revived people with nothing to rejoice about would be like a fresh batch with no chocolate chips, and nobody wants that batch.

The answer is that he will listen to what God will say, friends. He says, "I will listen to what God the LORD will say…" (Psalm 85:8). He did all that asking, and now he says he will listen. A lot of us ask and then start talking again before anybody answers. This singer says he's going to listen.
The word is peace, friends. The singer says, "…He will surely speak peace to His people and His saints…" (Psalm 85:8). Surely, he says. He's not guessing. He's sure of what God will speak.

The answer is False, friends. The singer says, "He will not let them return to folly." That's the end of verse 8, and it sits right beside God speaking peace (Psalm 85:8). The singer sounds sure of both.
The answer is True, friends: "Surely His salvation is near to those who fear Him…" (Psalm 85:9). Near is a good word. It's not far off, and it's not a rumor. The singer says it with confidence.

The word is kissed, friends: "righteousness and peace have kissed." It's a picture, and a sweet one (Psalm 85:10). Two things you might expect to be strangers meet like old friends. I love that the singer chose such a warm image.

The answers are earth and heaven, friends. "Faithfulness sprouts from the earth…" It comes up like a little green shoot out of the ground. And the other part of the picture comes from the other direction: "…righteousness looks down from heaven" (Psalm 85:11). So one thing comes up from the earth and another looks down from above, and both are in the same verse.

The answer is what is good, friends: "The LORD will indeed provide what is good, and our land will yield its increase." (Psalm 85:12). Indeed is the singer planting his flag. He isn't saying the LORD might provide good. He's saying it will happen, and I'd put that on a cookie box.

The answer is to prepare the way for His steps, friends. That's the last line of the song: "Righteousness will go before Him to prepare the way for His steps." (Psalm 85:13). Righteousness goes first and gets the road ready. I think it's a lovely way to close. Right where the psalm ends, it points to Him walking.
